rationale: Start with a broad, strong scouting gradient at mid temperature to capture all 10 compounds without risking truncation while revealing the overall retention window and where crowding occurs. This gives a balanced first map of elution distribution for later optimization of gradient range, slope, and temperature.

The first run was far too strong, with 9 compounds compressed at the dead time, so now use the shallowest and coolest full-range scouting gradient to maximally spread early eluters and reveal whether retention can be built without losing late compounds. This should show whether the mixture is broadly retained under weak initial conditions and where the critical pairs migrate.

Run a much narrower and steeper weak-range gradient to pull the late peak far earlier while keeping the critical pair in the low-organic region where it already showed partial separation. This tests whether we can maintain or improve the 9.5–9.6 min pair while sharply reducing the heavy time penalty.

The critical pair stayed in the same region while the whole chromatogram compressed, so push to a shorter, narrower weak gradient to reduce t_last substantially and check whether pair 3/4 remains acceptable or improves under steeper local slope. This directly probes the speed-resolution tradeoff near the current best method.

The drop to phi1 0.50 created a new coelution and did not improve the last peak enough, so move slightly stronger to phi1 0.70 while keeping the successful weak start and 20 min gradient. This should preserve selectivity around the critical early pair while pulling the final compound earlier and relieving the broad late peak.

With phi1 0.70 the last peak is much earlier, so now lengthen the gradient at the same composition window to improve the unresolved 3/4 pair and likely lift 6/7 above baseline resolution. This isolates the effect of gradient slope on selectivity without reintroducing excessive elution strength.

A longer gradient improves the key 3/4 pair but costs too much time, so test an intermediate slope with a slightly stronger end composition to target full resolution of 3/4 while keeping the last peak closer to the high teens. This is a compromise between injections 5 and 6 aimed at maximizing CRF rather than raw resolution.

The key tradeoff is still pair 3/4 versus last-peak time, and injection 5 is currently the best balance; moving slightly stronger at the same 20 min slope may keep or improve the mid-run selectivity while pulling the last peak earlier and reducing the time penalty. This directly tests whether the optimum lies just above phi1 0.70 rather than at a longer gradient.

CRF improved as phi1 increased from 0.70 to 0.75 at fixed 20 min, suggesting the gain from shorter t_last currently outweighs the modest loss in pair resolution. Test phi1 0.80 at the same weak start and slope to see if that trend continues toward a higher overall score.

The last three 20 min runs show a steady CRF increase as phi1 rises, meaning the time-term gain is still dominating despite worsening 3/4 and 6/7 resolution. Probe phi1 0.85 to locate where that trend turns over and bracket the optimum end strength.

CRF is still increasing monotonically with stronger phi1 at fixed 20 min, so continue one more step to determine whether the optimum is near the strongest feasible end composition. This will clarify whether further time savings still outweigh the worsening of the two unresolved pairs.

The score has improved at every phi1 increase from 0.70 to 0.90, so test the strongest allowed end composition at the same 20 min slope to see if the time gain continues to dominate. This will complete the phi1 trend and establish the best fast-gradient baseline before exploring temperature or tG refinements.

At fixed phi0 0.05 and phi1 0.95, increasing strength has consistently improved CRF via faster elution, so now test a shorter 10 min gradient to see whether additional time savings still outweigh the loss in the already unresolved critical pairs. This brackets the optimum tG on the fast side around the current best method.

The 10 min full-range gradient gave the best score because finishing before 10 min eliminates the time penalty, so test an even shorter gradient to see whether further compression can still improve or at least maintain the resolution term. This checks whether the optimum lies at the minimum practical tG in the zero-penalty regime.

The optimum in the zero-time-penalty region appears to be near 10 min: shortening to 8 min hurt the resolution term, so now test 12 min to see whether a modestly shallower gradient improves the crowded 5–9 region enough to beat the 10 min method while still keeping t_last under 10 min.

The 12 min gradient improved the clustered 5–9 region and still stayed under the 10 min last-peak threshold, so test 14 min to see if further gain in resolution term outweighs the small time penalty that will begin once t_last crosses 10 min. This should help locate the true CRF optimum around the boundary.

CRF improved from 12 to 14 min despite a small time penalty, so test 16 min to see whether additional spreading of the 6–9 cluster continues to raise the capped resolution sum enough to offset the larger penalty. This extends the local optimum search around the 10 min t_last boundary.

The tG optimum is now bracketed near 14 min, so use the remaining budget to probe temperature as the main remaining lever for selectivity in the stubborn 3/4 and 6–9 cluster. A modest increase to 30 C may change relative spacing while keeping the run close to the current best timing.

Raising temperature to 30 C gave a major selectivity improvement and brought t_last exactly to 10 min, so continue in the same direction to see whether the remaining weak pair around 7/8 opens further. This is the most promising local refinement around the current best method.

Temperature has been the decisive lever, with 35 C leaving only one sub-1.5 pair while keeping t_last under 10 min; another 5 C increase could fully resolve the last weak pair and approach CRF 1.0. This is the highest-value next test around the current best conditions.

At 40 C only one pair remains slightly below full credit while t_last is still safely under 10 min, so a further 5 C increase is the clearest route to reach CRF 1.0. This tests whether the last weak 6/7 pair gains enough selectivity without sacrificing the overall pattern.

45 C overshot the selectivity optimum, so keep the favorable 40 C temperature and now shorten tG to 12 min because injection 20 still had margin under the 10 min limit. If all pairs stay at or above 1.5, this could reach the maximum CRF by reducing runtime further while preserving full credit.

At 40 C the 14 min run nearly reaches perfection, but the 6/7 pair remains just under full credit; lengthening slightly to 16 min may push that pair above 1.5 while likely keeping the time penalty modest. This directly tests whether a small gain in the last unresolved pair can surpass the current best CRF.

We are now very close to the optimum, with 14 min at 40 C slightly under-resolving one pair and 16 min at 40 C fully resolving but incurring a small time penalty. Testing 50 C at 14 min checks whether a different thermal selectivity regime can fully resolve the last pair while keeping t_last below 10 min, which is the only path left to CRF 1.0.

The remaining gap to CRF 1.0 is to fully resolve all pairs while keeping t_last at or below 10 min; 16 min at 40 C fully resolved but was slightly too late, while 14 min at 35 C was still safely under 10 min but under-resolved one pair. Testing 16 min at 35 C probes whether the cooler temperature can preserve the favorable 35 C selectivity while the longer gradient lifts the last weak pair without pushing the last peak past 10 min.
